A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VWA-Adv research and retain identifiable attacks, experiments, and appendix material despite the changed title and substantial extension. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack experiments, cross-goal repeatability tests, synthetic-context experiments, and CLIP ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original text/image attack results, component-isolation experiments, and defense evaluations, alongside retained synthetic experiments and ablations.

M1.justification: v2 introduces ARE's procedure for representing agents as graphs and evaluating attack propagation through components. It also adds direct text injection and implemented defense pipelines involving paraphrasing and consistency checking. The original captioner PGD and CLIP ensemble optimization objectives remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the 200-task VWA-Adv benchmark covering classifieds, Reddit, and shopping, with retained adversarial-goal templates and synthetic image-selection scenarios. v2 adds an evaluated text-access scenario alongside bounded image perturbations, extending coverage within the existing web domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated reflexion and tree-search agents and comparisons involving safety prompting, abstention prompting, paraphrasing, and explicit consistency checking. These substantially expand the comparisons beyond v1's base, captioner-augmented, and self-captioning agents. The four backbone model families remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce component-edge evaluations and controls that selectively supply clean or adversarial captions. Reflexion permits two attempts, and tree search uses branching factor 3 and depth 1. v1's stepwise-versus-episode evaluation comparison is removed; v2 explicitly describes terminal-state evaluation. These additions establish new protocols without demonstrating reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled analyses of attacking the policy, evaluator, or value function separately and jointly, plus empirical defense tests. It removes v1's cross-goal repeatability study and stepwise-versus-episode validation. The resolution, negative-text, ensemble, and synthetic-context analyses are retained, partly relocated to Appendix C.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and both specify temperature-zero decoding. v1's removed 'Repeated ASR' experiment concerns transfer across user goals, rather than statistical uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o text-injection ASR of 40%, reflexion outcomes of 25% with a clean evaluator and 36% under joint attack, and corresponding tree-search outcomes of 26% and 38%. Paraphrasing reduces ASR from 31% to 27.5%. Earlier goal-specific tables and repeatability results disappear, while synthetic-context and CLIP-ablation values remain unchanged. The differently grouped headline rates are not directly comparable performance changes.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3 introduces formal agent graphs, adversarial influence AdvIn(c), expected edge weights, a deterministic-environment assumption, and conventions for unexecuted branches. This is substantial new mathematical formulation beyond v1's attack objectives, although it does not add theorem proofs.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on captioner and CLIP attacks demonstrating agent vulnerability. v2 makes ARE and component-level robustness central contributions, extending its main claims to reflexion and tree-search agents and to how additional components can either block or amplify attacks.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving adversarial verification, reflections, and value scores, and qualifies defensive benefits by whether components themselves are compromised. Appendix D newly characterizes attack results as lower bounds on risk and limits conclusions to the evaluated agent algorithms. v1's vision-only limitation is replaced as text attacks enter the study.

D1.justification: v2 adds evaluation-matching rules, safety-prompt excerpts, and configuration details for the new agent studies. It omits v1's explicit PGD initialization and checkpoint-selection descriptions, including GPT-4 scoring of CLIP candidates. Model identifiers, hardware, and the code/data repository remain unchanged; omitted details do not establish changed attack implementations.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around compound-agent robustness and distinguishes it from concurrent AgentDojo and EIA research. Related work expands to indirect prompt injection, Agent Smith, defense methods, and the tree-search agent, supporting the shift beyond v1's emphasis on image attacks and captioner vulnerabilities.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The setup, method, and experimental narrative are reorganized around ARE and component robustness, replacing v1's attack-centered organization. Several retained explanations move to appendices, while much appendix implementation material remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 replaces much of the main results presentation with agent graphs, weighted attack-propagation diagrams, a robustness-utility scatterplot, and a defense bar chart. Earlier detailed result tables and attack examples are removed. The resolution heatmap moves to the appendix, while several agent illustrations and appendix tables are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for system-level conclusions: Sections 5.2–5.4 isolate how evaluators and value functions block or amplify attacks and empirically test defense ideas that v1 largely proposed. ARE provides a common framework for these comparisons. These gains outweigh the loss of repeatability evidence, detailed result tables, and some optimization documentation. Reporting weaknesses remain, including introductory relative-change percentages that do not consistently match the displayed results.
